title: When looking away means looking inward: contextual interpretation of gaze aversions determines their attentional value.
abstract: Eye movements are typically understood as supporting outward orienting, directing attention toward locations of interest in the external environment. However, not all eye movements reflect outward orienting. Gaze aversions, the common tendency to look away during effortful cognitive processing, serve as social signals of inward-oriented attention and ongoing processing. Because observers continuously monitor others' eye movements and use gaze-related cues to guide their own behavior, distinguishing between outward-oriented gaze-shifts and inward-oriented gaze aversions is a basic challenge in human interaction. Here, we examine the hypothesis that this distinction depends on the context in which gaze shifts appear. While participants reorient their attention following an outward-oriented gaze shift, they withhold doing so when the context suggests that the gaze shift reflects inward-oriented processing. To test this hypothesis, we relied on the Gaze Cueing Effect (GCE), an attentional orienting to observed gaze shifts that is known to be modulated by top-down context and interpretation. In two pre-registered experiments (total N = 90), participants performed a gaze-cueing letter-discrimination task while viewing identical gaze shifts within different contexts. One group was led to interpret the gaze shifts as occurring during effortful thinking, whereas the other group received no thinking-related context. Across both experiments, attentional orienting was significantly reduced when gaze shifts were perceived as reflecting internal cognitive processing rather than attention shifts. These findings demonstrate that gaze aversions function as communicative signals that dynamically regulate interpersonal attention, and that gaze following depends fundamentally on the inferred social meaning of the observed eye movement.

title: The relation of whole-brain functional connectivity to global amyloid and local tau presence.
abstract: Previous neuroimaging studies have demonstrated that beta-amyloid (Aβ) plaques and neurofibrillary tangles of tau are associated with disruptions in neurocognitive function in Alzheimer's disease. However, the relationship between Aβ, tau deposition, and functional network connectivity in normal aging and mild cognitive impairment remains unclear. Using resting-state functional MRI and Aβ PET and tau PET data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we applied multiple regression models to examine the independent and interactive effects of Aβ and tau on network connectivity and cognitive performance across 297 participants who are considered clinically normal or mildly impaired but not demented. Higher Aβ burden was associated with greater within-network connectivity, particularly in frontoparietal, somatomotor, and salience networks. In contrast, higher tau levels were associated with lower within-network connectivity in default mode and limbic networks. Despite weak evidence of continuous Aβ × tau interaction, tau associations exhibited descriptively distinct patterns in Aβ-negative and Aβ-positive individuals in the exploratory stratified analyses. In visual and limbic networks, negative associations between tau and functional connectivity were most evident among Aβ-negative individuals. Furthermore, mediation analyses revealed a suppressor pattern involving the somatomotor network connectivity that alleviated the negative association between Aβ burden and cognitive performance. These findings suggest Aβ and tau have both distinct and interactive impacts on large-scale brain networks and cognition. Further understanding of the differential effects of these pathological proteins on the longitudinal trajectories of functional networks and neurocognitive functions may help inform the development of targeted interventions aimed at preserving network integrity and slowing cognitive decline before dementia.

title: Targeting the DFG-out conformation of TTBK1 enables the discovery of selective type II neuroprotective inhibitors.
abstract: Tau Tubulin Kinase 1 (TTBK1) is an emerging therapeutic target for neurodegenerative diseases because it promotes the pathological phosphorylation of tau and TDP-43, key drivers of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, the development of selective TTBK1 inhibitors is hindered by the high structural similarity between TTBK1 and the essential paralog TTBK2, making ATP-competitive strategies challenging. Here, we report the discovery of computationally supported type II TTBK1 inhibitors by targeting the inactive DFG-out kinase conformation. A druggable DFG-out model was generated using metadynamics and molecular dynamic simulations and employed for virtual screening of the MBC chemical library. This approach identified novel chemotypes that were validated as selective TTBK1 inhibitors with improved discrimination over TTBK2. The most promising compounds also displayed neuroprotective activity in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells. These findings demonstrate that targeting the inactive TTBK1 conformation is a viable strategy to achieve isoform selectivity and establish a new framework for developing disease-modifying therapies for ALS, AD, and other TTBK1-driven neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Thermoresponsive chitosan/silk fibroin/PVA/PVP hydrogel loaded with BDNF promotes functional recovery after stroke.
abstract: Stroke remains a leading cause of adult disability, driven in part by the formation of a non-permissive extracellular matrix environment that limits endogenous repair. Injectable biomaterials that can modulate this microenvironment while enabling localized therapeutic delivery represent a promising strategy for post-stroke brain regeneration. Here, we report the development of a thermoresponsive hybrid hydrogel composed of chitosan, β-glycerophosphate, silk fibroin, polyvinyl alcohol and polyvinyl pyrrolidone, engineered to provide tunable physicochemical properties and enhanced biological functionalities for intracerebral implantation. Systematic optimization identified a formulation (F6) that exhibited rapid gelation at physiological temperature, appropriate viscoelastic properties, a microporous architecture, and in vitro biodegradation, conducive to cellular infiltration and molecular transport. In a mouse model of photothrombotic stroke, intracerebral delivery of the F6 hydrogel attenuated reactive astrogliosis and microglial activation in the peri-infarct region, while enhancing neurogenesis in the subventricular zone. Notably, incorporation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor within the hydrogel significantly improved functional recovery over 8 weeks, demonstrating the capacity of this hydrogel to act as a localized delivery platform for neuro-regenerative therapeutics. Together, this study establishes a tunable thermoresponsive hydrogel platform that integrates structural support with localized therapeutic delivery, highlighting its potential as a minimally invasive strategy for modulating the post-stroke microenvironment and promoting functional recovery.

title: Combining brain-penetrating and anticancer peptides into bivalent-branched peptides conserves brain targeting and improves activity in vitro.
abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is a particularly challenging subtype of breast cancer (BC) due to the absence of common therapeutically targetable receptors, its tendency toward chemoresistance, and its high rates of recurrence and metastasis, particularly to the brain. The development of brain metastases (BM) poses an additional hurdle, largely due to the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Recently, we reported the therapeutic potential of a dual-acting peptide, PepH3-vCPP2319, that combines a BBB peptide shuttle (BBBpS - PepH3) and an anticancer peptide (ACP - vCPP2319) to eliminate TNBC-BM. In vitro, PepH3-vCPP2319 showed high translocation capacity in our transwell system (BBB cross > 40%), high anticancer activity (IC50 ∼ 5.0 µM), and low toxicity (HC50 > 25.0 µM). To further enhance its potency, we designed two bivalent-branched peptides that conjugate two PepH3 sequences and one vCPP2319 sequence, or vice versa. Our results indicated that, compared with PepH3-vCPP2319, both peptides translocated (∼ 40%) across a cellular BBB model and exhibited stronger anticancer activity (IC50 ∼ 2.0 µM) while maintaining moderate toxicity (HC50 > 15.0 µM). Compared with vCPP2319 and PepH3-vCPP2319, both bivalent-branched peptides are internalized quicker in cancer cells without membrane disruption, suggesting an intracellular mechanism of action. In conclusion, our study demonstrates the merit of branched peptide design in keeping the brain delivery and improving the efficacy of ACPs, although with slightly high toxicity, for the treatment of TNBC-BM.

title: Generation of induced pluripotent stem cell lines from two patients with CLIFAHDD syndrome.
abstract: CLIFAHDD (Congenital Contractures of the Limbs and Face, Hypotonia, and Developmental Delay, OMIM #616266) is a neurodevelopmental disorder resulting from gain-of-function variants in NALCN, the gene encoding the sodium leak channel. Patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines were generated from two patients with CLIFAHDD due to de novo NALCN variants: c.965 T > C p.(Ile322Thr) on exon 9 and c.1798 G > C p.(Asp600His) on exon 15. The variants have been characterized by neurophysiology models of NALCN, which confirmed gain-of function in the NALCN ion channel. These iPSC lines will be a powerful resource for the study of CLIFAHDD and the NALCN channelosome.

title: Inhalation of Gardenia jasminoides flower essential oil attenuates stress-associated neurobehavioral abnormalities in mice.
journal: Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology
abstract: Gardenia jasminoides Ellis is a traditional medicinal and aromatic plant, but the neurobehavioral potential of its flower-derived essential oil remains insufficiently understood. This study aimed to evaluate whether G. jasminoides flower essential oil (GEO) inhalation attenuates chronic stress-associated neurobehavioral abnormalities and to characterize the accompanying hippocampal, metabolic, and gut microbial responses. GEO was chemically profiled by headspace solid-phase microextraction coupled with gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and evaluated in a chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) mouse model. Mice were exposed to GEO by inhalation during the final 2 weeks of the 6-week CUMS procedure. Behavioral performance was assessed using the open field test, elevated plus maze, tail suspension test, forced swim test, and sucrose preference test. Hippocampal morphology, inflammatory and oxidative stress-related indices, neurochemical markers, serum corticosterone, serum metabolomics, hippocampal transcriptomics, gut microbiota composition, and hippocampal neuroimmune/synaptic signaling markers were further analyzed. Chemical profiling tentatively annotated 59 volatile constituents in GEO, with linalool and linalyl acetate identified as the predominant constituents. GEO inhalation attenuated CUMS-associated behavioral abnormalities, with significant changes observed most consistently in the GEO-20 group. GEO exposure was also associated with increased hippocampal dendritic spine density relative to the CUMS group, lower inflammatory and oxidative stress-related indices, higher hippocampal brain-derived neurotrophic factor, γ-aminobutyric acid, and 5-hydroxytryptamine levels, and lower serum corticosterone. Serum metabolomics identified GEO-20-associated changes in metabolic features and pathways involving nucleotide/purine metabolism, arachidonic acid-related lipid mediator pathways, bile acid-related metabolism, and neuroactive metabolic processes. Hippocampal transcriptomics identified GEO-20-associated changes in neuroimmune-, neuroactive ligand-receptor-, and γ-aminobutyric acid synapse-related transcriptional profiles. Gut microbiota analysis revealed GEO-20-associated changes in microbial richness, community composition, discriminatory taxa, and genus-level co-occurrence patterns. Targeted molecular assays showed lower hippocampal glial reactivity and inflammatory signaling-related markers after GEO exposure, whereas GEO-20 was associated with higher levels of mitochondrial regulatory and synaptic plasticity markers. GEO inhalation attenuated chronic stress-associated neurobehavioral abnormalities in mice and was accompanied by changes in hippocampal neuroimmune and synaptic plasticity-related markers, together with broader systemic metabolic and microbial responses.

title: Physiological insights and clinical evidence of high flow nasal cannula as first-line therapy for acute hypercapnic exacerbation of COPD: a narrative review.
abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a common lung disease. Acute exacerbations (AECOPD) are associated with increased hospitalisations and mortality. Current guidelines provide only conditional recommendation for the use of High Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC) supported by low-certainty evidence in hypercapnic respiratory failure. Since then, additional studies have been published, and we aimed to review the available literature on HFNC as a first-line therapy in hypercapnic AECOPD. Structured literature research was performed in PubMed and Embase to include studies assessing HFNC as a first-line therapy in hypercapnic AECOPD and focusing on clinical outcomes (dyspnoea, blood gas, treatment failure, mortality). Studies were categorized as single-arm studies, comparisons with conventional oxygen therapy (COT), or comparisons with non-invasive ventilation (NIV). Among 17 articles included, 2 were uncontrolled, 3 articles compared HFNC to COT and 12 compared HFNC to NIV. HFNC was often associated with better comfort and tolerance. Compared to COT, HFNC might reduce treatment failure, but evidence is still scarce. Compared to NIV, HFNC had similar effects on dyspnoea and blood gas analysis in most studies, but it remains uncertain considering treatment failure. In hypercapnic AECOPD, HFNC remains an alternative therapeutic option as compared to COT but also to NIV when the latter is contraindicated, not tolerated or during breaks from NIV. Further research is warranted with well-designed RCT focusing on treatment failure and mortality. In the future, patients might be selected considering some endotypes of AECOPD such as bronchorrhea, sleep apnea overlap or disproportionate dyspnoea which could benefit differently from HFNC.

title: Valence and expectation effects shape event-related potentials to probabilistic social-evaluative feedback from putative peers.
journal: Cortex; a journal devoted to the study of the nervous system and behavior
abstract: In everyday life, we receive social evaluative feedback from specific interaction partners that shapes our expectations about future feedback. It has been proposed that feedback processing and expectations are biased toward positive social feedback. However, the neuronal processes underlying biased social feedback processing remain unclear. In the current Event-Related Potentials (ERPs) study, we exposed participants to seemingly real social evaluations from three senders, each providing dichotomous positive or negative feedback on trait adjectives. In reality, feedback contingencies were manipulated with different ratios of positive versus negative feedback (rare 20 vs 80; equal 50 vs 50; frequent 80 vs 20 per cent of all trials). Participants' expectation ratings followed the general feedback ratios, though they indicated higher expectations for positive feedback. A lower probability of feedback increased all investigated ERP components, except the P1. Furthermore, positive versus negative feedback led to relatively more positive amplitudes in the Feedback-Related Negativity (FRN) and Late Positive Potential (LPP) time windows. Interactions between valence and probability were found for exploratory analyses of the Early Posterior Negativity (EPN) and theory-driven analyses of the P3, with specifically increased amplitudes for rare negative feedback compared to rare positive feedback. The results suggest that, even though negative feedback elicited higher prediction-error-related effects in ERPs associated with general surprise responses (P3) and perceptual attentional enhancement (EPN), the LPP, which is related to elaborate processing, integration, and updating, exhibited larger amplitudes for positive feedback, possibly reflecting biased processing of positive feedback. This may be fundamental for maintaining a positively biased self-view.

title: Conflict between representational formats and procedures constrains visual tracking.
abstract: Computer-assisted design software, such as PowerPoint, groups separate elements to create structured objects whose parts can be manipulated relative to the whole. Might visual perception perform a similar operation, grouping scene elements and representing them with internal reference to the emergent structure? The proposal is central yet perennially controversial in cognitive neuroscience and philosophy of mind. In a series of seven preregistered tracking experiments, we identify internally referenced representations in human vision by relying on the logic that, as in computer-assisted design, a representation will make certain procedures easy to access while limiting others. Participants tracked a target among identical nontargets organized into geometric shapes. When the shapes rotated, performance was high, suggesting the use of internally referenced, shape-centered representations that naturally support rotational transformations. In contrast, performance declined in translation conditions, where constituent items moved independently, revealing a mismatch between the internally structured representation and the requisite, externally oriented tracking procedure. This effect replicated across diverse stimuli, including occluded, rounded, and irregular shapes, and was reduced when structure-inducing cues were disrupted. These findings identify representational format and its compatibility with task procedures as an important determinant of visual performance.

title: CSF pTau181 predicts asymmetric hippocampal atrophy in cognitively unimpaired older adults.
journal: The journal of prevention of Alzheimer's disease
abstract: Hippocampal atrophy is a core marker of neurodegeneration in dementia, particularly in Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, most studies focus on total hippocampal volume loss and overlook hemispheric asymmetry, which may reflect distinct biological processes. While tau pathology is closely linked to medial temporal lobe degeneration, it remains unclear whether tau is associated with asymmetric patterns of hippocampal atrophy. We analyzed 483 cognitively unimpaired participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) with baseline cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) phosphorylated tau (pTau181) and amyloid-β (Aβ42) measurements and longitudinal structural MRI data over 10 years of follow-up. Total hippocampal volume and hemispheric asymmetry, defined as the absolute difference between left and right hippocampal volumes (|L-R|), were quantified at each visit. Linear mixed-effects models assessed associations between baseline CSF biomarkers and longitudinal changes in hippocampal asymmetry, adjusting for demographic factors, APOE ε4 status, and baseline hippocampal volume. Higher baseline CSF pTau181 was associated with greater increases in hippocampal asymmetry over time (β = 1.20, SE = 0.43, p = 0.006). This association remained significant after additional adjustment for total hippocampal volume and baseline CSF Aβ42. CSF total tau was highly correlated with pTau181 (Spearman's ρ =0.98, p < 0.001) and showed comparable associations with hippocampal measures. In contrast, baseline Aβ42 was not associated with subsequent changes in hippocampal asymmetry. Both pTau181 and Aβ42 were associated with faster decline in total hippocampal volume. In amyloid-stratified analyses, pTau181 was associated with increasing hippocampal asymmetry only among amyloid-negative individuals, whereas its association with total hippocampal atrophy was observed primarily in amyloid-positive individuals. CSF pTau181 is associated not only with overall hippocampal atrophy but also with progressive hippocampal asymmetry, suggesting that tau-related neurodegeneration may manifest as both magnitude and imbalance of tissue loss. These findings support hippocampal asymmetry as a complementary neuroimaging marker that may capture medial temporal lobe neurodegeneration in cognitively unimpaired older adults, with potential applications in early disease risk stratification, longitudinal disease monitoring, and the identification of biologically distinct participants for future clinical trials.

title: Monte Carlo simulation of a neuroimaging acquisition with MAPSSIC, a β+sensitive intracerebral microprobe for awake and freely moving rats.
abstract: Establishing robust correlations between molecular neuroimaging and behavioral studies is essential in preclinical research to advance our understanding of brain function and to critically assess the translational relevance of animal models in drug development.Achieving this goal, however, requires imaging animals while they are awake and freely moving -an ongoing challenge, as most preclinical imaging techniques rely on anesthesia.Approach: To overcome the limitations imposed by anesthesia, the MAPSSIC project aims to develop a novel implantable pixelated probe based on Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS), designed for use in awake, freely moving rats. By virtue of its direct implantation within the targeted brain regions, the MAPSSIC probe enables the local detection of short-range β+particles emitted by radiotracers, in contrast to conventional micro-PET systems that rely on detecting coincident annihilation γ-rays. In this study, we present Monte Carlo simulations of a typical in vivo brain imaging experiment using [11C]Raclopride, a commonly employed β+-emitting radiotracer, to evaluate the probe's performance.Main results: Results show that over 93 % of detected events originate from particles emitted within the first 2 mm surrounding the probe while also allowing to quantify variations of 5 % to 30 % of the non-displaceable binding potential (BPND) with discrepancy of less than 4 % compared to micro-PET.Significance: This Monte Carlo study demonstrates the device's ability to capture small variations of BPNDbased on spatially localized information, validating its suitability for quantitative kinetic analysis in brain structures such as the striatum.

title: The Effect of Bipolar Disorder Illness Course on Physiological Digital Signals: Observational Study.
abstract: Although bipolar disorder (BD) lacks objective biomarkers of illness progression, wearable devices enable continuous, real-world collection of physiological digital biosignals, offering a promising approach to address this gap. Measures such as electrodermal activity (EDA) and heart rate variability (HRV) fluctuate with mood state and symptom severity. Previous studies have reported reduced EDA during depressive episodes and increased HRV following symptom resolution after acute mood episodes. Furthermore, greater illness burden in BD has been associated with lower HRV, suggesting that digital biosignals may capture not only state-related changes but also aspects of illness course. This study investigated whether naturalistic EDA and heart rate (HR) profiles differ according to illness course variables in BD-including diagnosis, predominant polarity, years since onset, and lifetime number of episodes-in euthymic patients, to evaluate their potential as illness course biomarkers. This cross-sectional post hoc analysis used data from 80 euthymic patients on the BD spectrum from the INTREPIBD-TIMEBASE cohort. Participants were recruited at Hospital Clínic de Barcelona (Spain) between 2021 and 2024 and wore an Empatica E4 wristband for 48 hours in naturalistic settings. Inclusion criteria comprised a current or past DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition) diagnosis of BD confirmed by structured interview and sustained euthymia. We examined the effects of 4 illness course variables (diagnosis, predominant polarity, years since onset, and number of lifetime episodes) on 3 biosignals (mean EDA, EDA peaks per minute, and HR) using generalized additive models. Interactions between illness course variables and circadian patterns were also assessed. All models were adjusted for age, sex, and current antipsychotic use and included a participant-specific random effect. Of the 80 participants, 49 (61.3%) were female; participants' mean age was 46.9 (SD 14.1) years. After adjustment for covariates and multiple comparisons, no significant associations were observed between illness course variables and EDA or HR. In sensitivity analyses excluding patients with schizoaffective disorder (n=75), years since illness onset and predominant polarity were associated with EDA peaks per minute after multiple comparison correction. Specifically, patients with more than 22 years since illness onset had fewer EDA peaks compared with other groups (β=-1.06, 95% CI -1.71 to -0.41; P=.001). No significant interactions were found between illness course variables and circadian patterns of EDA or HR. To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the association between illness course variables and EDA and HR recorded in naturalistic settings in BD. In contrast to prior findings linking illness burden with HRV, our results suggest that years since illness onset may show modest associations with phasic EDA activity. These findings indicate that digital biosignals may be more sensitive to state-related changes than to illness course characteristics, limiting their use as longitudinal biomarkers of disease progression.

title: CogniPaz, an Ecologically Oriented Gamified mHealth Tool for Detecting Mild Cognitive Impairment: Prospective Cohort Diagnostic Accuracy Study.
abstract: Discriminating mild cognitive impairment (MCI) from subjective cognitive decline (SCD), and healthy controls (HC) remains challenging. Digital tools may overcome paper-and-pencil screening's limitations. This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy and usability of CogniPaz (Daniel Blanco), an ecologically oriented, mobile health (mHealth), gamified cognitive assessment tool exploring memory and executive functions, in discriminating MCI (particularly amnestic phenotypes [aMCI]) from SCD, and HC. This prospective observational study recruited a convenience sample of consecutive patients with cognitive complaints and HC at La Paz University Hospital Cognitive Disorders Unit from April 2025 to January 2026. Demographic and clinical characteristics, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores were collected. An evaluator blinded to the MoCA scores oversaw the automated, self-administered CogniPaz assessment. Participants were classified into HC (no cognitive complaints, MoCA score≥26), SCD (cognitive complaints, MoCA score≥26), and MCI (cognitive complaints without functional impairment, MoCA score<26, subdivided into amnestic [aMCI] and nonamnestic phenotypes). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses using age-adjusted models, the DeLong test, and bootstrap validation evaluated diagnostic accuracy across groups. The correlation between MoCA and CogniPaz scores was assessed using Spearman rank correlation. Participants with available biomarker data underwent exploratory analysis of CogniPaz's ability to detect biologically confirmed any-cause neurodegeneration (bND). Usability was tested using an ad hoc Likert questionnaire (1-9 points). The participants (n=84, 57.1% female; median age 72.0, IQR 62.5-77.0 years) included 27 HC, 17 with SCD, 22 with aMCI, and 18 with nonamnestic MCI. The aMCI group was older than the SCD group (age: median 76.5, IQR 70.8-78.8 vs median 59.0, IQR 50.0-69.0 years; Kruskal-Wallis/Dunn, P=.003). CogniPaz scores correlated with MoCA scores (ρ=0.81, 95% CI 0.75-0.89; P<.001). CogniPaz showed good concurrent accuracy, independently of age: MCI vs HC (area under the curve [AUC]=0.880, 95% CI 0.798-0.961), MCI vs SCD (AUC=0.915, 95% CI 0.841-0.990), aMCI vs HC (AUC=0.910, 95% CI 0.830-0.990), and aMCI vs SCD (AUC=0.943, 95% CI 0.878-1.000). At the provisional <28.5 cutoff point, sensitivity ranged from 85.0% (34/40, 95% CI 70.2-94.3) to 90.9% (20/22, 95% CI 70.8-98.9) and specificity from 74.1% (20/27, 95% CI 53.7-88.9) to 82.4% (14/17, 95% CI 56.6-96.2) across comparisons. CogniPaz suggested capacity to detect bND (AUC=0.810, 95% CI 0.661-0.958), with potential incremental value over MoCA and age (odds ratio [OR]=0.78, 95% CI 0.60-0.94; P=.02). Median administration time was 9.39 (IQR 7.53-11.38) minutes with 100% (84/84) completion. User satisfaction was high (median score 8.4/9, IQR 7.9-8.6; Cronbach α=0.84). CogniPaz is an innovative, user-friendly mHealth tool that addresses classical cognitive screening tools' limitations through a brief, multidomain, minimally supervised gamified format, with high patient acceptance. It correlates with MoCA scores, shows good concurrent capacity to differentiate MCI, particularly aMCI, from SCD and HC, and appears promising for identifying bND. Pending external longitudinal validation, these findings support CogniPaz as a candidate for early cognitive screening in primary care.

title: Are negative findings gaining ground at ECNP congresses? A 10-year analysis.
journal: European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology

title: Occupational Exposure to Petroleum-Derived Lubricants and Risk of Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: Lung irritants such as smoking and organic solvents are established risk factors of multiple sclerosis (MS), with effects influenced by genetic susceptibility, particularly leukocyte antigen (HLA) DRB1*15:01 and HLA-A*02:01. Petroleum-derived lubricants represent another widespread occupational exposure with potential inflammatory properties, yet their contribution to MS etiology remains unclear. This study investigated associations between occupational exposure to petroleum-based lubricants and MS risk, including interactions with smoking and HLA genotypes. This investigation was based on a Swedish population-based case-control design. Incident MS cases were consecutively recruited by neurologists at 40 clinics (2005-2015). Inclusion criteria comprised residence in Sweden, age 16-70 years, and a diagnosis of MS confirmed by a neurologist according to the McDonald criteria. Controls were randomly selected from the national population register using density sampling and frequency-matched to cases by age, sex, and residential area. Exposure to petroleum-derived lubricants was assessed using questionnaire data. Logistic regression was used to estimate odds ratios (ORs) and 95% CIs for MS in relation to occupational exposure to petroleum-derived lubricants. Interactions with smoking, HLA-DRB1*15:01, and absence of HLA-A*02:01 were assessed on the additive scale using the attributable proportion due to interaction (AP). The study population comprised 2,872 incident MS cases and 6,122 controls (mean age: 34.6 years; 72% female). Occupational exposure to petroleum-derived lubricants was associated with increased MS risk (OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.16-1.65), with a modest exposure-duration response. The association persisted when applying a 7-year exposure lag (OR 1.55, 95% CI 1.27-1.90). A positive interaction was identified between petroleum exposure and smoking (AP 0.34, 95% CI 0.10-0.55). Among the subset with available HLA data (2,070 cases and 2,899 controls), petroleum exposure interacted with the absence of HLA-A*02:01 (AP 0.32, 95% CI 0.05-0.59). A similar interaction was observed with HLA-DRB1*15:01 (AP 0.19, 95% CI -0.08-0.46), although this estimate did not reach statistical significance. Occupational exposure to petroleum-derived lubricants was associated with MS risk, with stronger associations among smokers and participants with established genetic susceptibility. These findings add to the evidence that lung irritants and gene-environment interactions contribute to MS susceptibility but require replication in independent populations.

title: Reproductive Lifespan and Hormonal Therapy in Relation to Later-Life Neurovascular Health in Community-Dwelling Older Women.
abstract: Women are disproportionately affected by Alzheimer disease (AD), a vulnerability that may relate to estrogen fluctuations across the lifespan. Estrogen has neuroprotective and vasoprotective effects, suggesting that lifetime estrogen exposure may influence both AD-related neurodegeneration and cerebrovascular health. However, its association with late-life vascular and neurodegenerative brain changes remains unclear. We aimed to examine the associations of lifelong estrogen exposure-endogenous (reproductive span) and exogenous (oral contraceptives [OCs], menopausal hormone therapy [MHT])-with late-life vascular brain injury and AD-related atrophy and explore apolipoprotein-ε4 (APOE-ε4) effects. This population-based study included cognitively unimpaired women from the Gothenburg H70-1944 Birth Cohort who underwent brain MRI at age 70 and again 5 years later. Reproductive lifespan was calculated as age at menopause or oophorectomy minus age at menarche. OC and MHT use were categorized as ever vs never users. Outcomes included cerebral small vessel disease (SVD), AD-related cortical thickness, and white matter integrity (fractional anisotropy). SVD burden was a composite score derived from white matter hyperintensities (WMHs), lacunes, cerebral microbleeds (CMBs), and perivascular spaces (PVSs) (range 0-4). Linear, multinomial, and mixed-effects regression models were adjusted for relevant confounders and stratified by APOE-ε4. Among 352 women (mean age 70 years), longer reproductive span was associated with lower SVD burden (OR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.86-0.99). MHT use was associated with fewer PVSs and CMBs. OC and MHT use were associated with greater white matter integrity, with combined use showing the highest fractional anisotropy compared with nonusers (β = 0.45, 95% CI 0.12-0.78). No multiplicative interaction between OCs and MHT was observed, although joint exposure analyses suggested cumulative effects. MHT use was associated with greater AD-related cortical thickness among APOE-ε4 carriers only (β = 0.38, 95% CI 0.01-0.76). Longer estrogen exposure was associated with stable cortical thickness and WMH trajectories over time. Greater lifetime estrogen exposure, both endogenous and exogenous, was associated with lower cerebrovascular pathology in women and, among APOE-ε4 carriers, greater cortical thickness in AD-vulnerable regions. These findings support the potential role of cerebrovascular mechanisms linking estrogen exposure to brain aging. Limitations included observational design and self-reported, binary estrogen exposure. Potential cognitive effects require further studies.

title: Stability of eye movement-related eardrum oscillations to acoustic and gravitational/postural manipulations.
abstract: Recent studies describe Eye Movement-Related Eardrum Oscillations (EMREOs), low‑frequency signals recorded in the ear canal that arise from the tympanic membrane and are triggered by saccadic eye movements. Because EMREOs are thought to arise from motor elements in the peripheral auditory system, we examined how two known modulators of these elements affect the EMREO time course. First, the activity of outer hair cells (OHCs) can be suppressed by the medial olivocochlear reflex (MOCR). If OHCs contribute to the generation of EMREOs, activation of this reflex should reduce EMREO amplitude. To test this, we compared EMREO amplitudes elicited by saccades performed in silence and in the presence of contralateral noise. Second, postural (i.e., vestibular and proprioceptive) cues linked to head orientation may influence EMREOs via oculomotor control circuits that possibly modulate middle ear muscles. To test this, we recorded EMREOs while participants made saccades with their head upright (0° azimuth) and with their head tilted 30° in either direction. Across both experiments our data reveal no significant modulation of the EMREO by these experimental manipulations. Together with other recent studies these findings advocate for a stability of the EMREO towards multiple experimental modulations. We discuss how this fuels speculations that the signal may serve as a temporal reference frame, while also being compatible with the notion that the EMREO reflects a spatial coordinate transform for combining signals across the senses.

title: Bayesian efficient coding.
abstract: The efficient coding hypothesis, which proposes that neurons are optimized to maximize information about the environment, has provided a guiding theoretical framework for sensory and systems neuroscience. More recently, a theory known as the Bayesian Brain hypothesis has focused on the brain's ability to integrate sensory and prior sources of information in order to perform Bayesian inference. Although pieces of a connection between these two hypotheses have appeared in prior work, a general formulation that treats the optimality criterion as an arbitrary functional of the posterior distribution - and thereby admits both information-based and other objectives within a single framework - has remained largely implicit. Here we make this formulation explicit, developing a Bayesian theory of efficient coding that defines Bayesian efficient codes in terms of four basic ingredients: (1) a stimulus prior distribution; (2) an encoding model; (3) a capacity constraint, specifying a neural resource limit; and (4) a loss functional, quantifying the desirability or undesirability of various posterior distributions. Classic efficient codes arise as the special case in which the loss functional is the posterior entropy, leading to a code that maximizes mutual information, but alternate loss functionals give solutions that differ dramatically from information-maximizing codes. Within this framework we introduce covtropy, a novel family of losses defined on posterior distributions and parameterized by a single exponent, and use it to show that decorrelation of sensory inputs - optimal under classic efficient codes in low-noise settings - can be disadvantageous for objectives that penalize large errors. We then reanalyze Laughlin's seminal data on contrast coding in the blowfly large monopolar cell, and find that the measured response nonlinearity is better explained by minimizing Lp reconstruction error with p = 1/2 than by information maximization, overturning a forty-year-old interpretation. Bayesian efficient coding thus enlarges the family of codes that are optimal under different objectives and provides a more general framework for understanding the design principles of sensory systems.

title: Saccadic suppression enhances saliency of ecologically relevant stimuli in the zebrafish optic tectum.
abstract: Saccadic suppression, a reduction in visual sensitivity around the time of rapid eye movements, is well-documented in primate psychophysics, but its mechanisms and functions remain debated. Here, we use zebrafish to trace the origins of saccadic suppression, and we demonstrate how saccadic suppression selectively enhances the visual salience of ecologically relevant stimuli. Saccadic suppression thus contributes to more than just compensation for rapid saccade-induced image shifts. We first established a behavioral correlate of saccadic suppression in larval zebrafish escape behavior. Then, using electrophysiology, we show that retinal ganglion cells jumpstart saccadic suppression in a spatial frequency-dependent manner. Calcium imaging, combined with 360° visual stimulation and behavioral tracking, revealed that motor signals enhance peri-saccadic suppression strength in the optic tectum, where suppression lasts for more than 3,000 ms. Notably, saccadic suppression is much weaker and more short-lived for stimuli related to hunting or escape behavior than for behaviorally less relevant global flashes. This unequal attenuation effectively increases the salience of the ecologically relevant stimuli in the optic tectum after saccades. Our results demonstrate that saccadic suppression integrates visual and motor signals to optimize sensory processing within neural constraints, and they provide insights into evolutionarily conserved visual strategies.

title: Distinct tau PET dynamics in early versus late age-of-onset Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD) and late-onset AD (LOAD) differ in clinical presentations and rates of progression. We aimed to compare baseline and longitudinal tau positron emission tomography (PET) burden measured with 18F-flortaucipir and its relationship with clinical variables in amyloid PET-positive, cognitively impaired participants from the Longitudinal Early-Onset Alzheimer's Disease Study (EOAD; n = 390) and Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (LOAD; n = 211). Participants with EOAD showed higher baseline tau PET burden, broader neuroanatomical involvement, and stronger associations of tau PET with amyloid PET and global cognition. Higher baseline tau PET burden in EOAD was independently validated in participants with EOAD from ADNI. Longitudinally, tau PET increased more rapidly in EOAD than in LOAD, independent of amyloid PET and clinical stage. We conclude that earlier age of onset in AD is linked to a more aggressive tauopathy, which in turn is a primary driver of clinical decline.

title: Lighting up necrotic neurons from traumatic brain injury with magnetic quantum dots to decode the cellular origin of MRI.
abstract: The diagnosis of traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains heavily constrained by the limitations of conventional imaging techniques in visualizing the pathological events that determine the disease progression and outcome. To address this clinical challenge, we report a manganese-doped near-infrared quantum dot (QD) to intrinsically integrate the highly sensitive optical imaging with clinical compatible magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Taking the advantages of optical imaging powered by whole-brain clearing and cellular resolution three-dimensional (3D) panoptic imaging, in combination with the systematic in vitro cell studies on different types of cells involved in TBI, we disclosed the interpretable pathology reflected by TBI imaging through the highly sensitive fluorescence of magnetic QDs, i.e., after systemic administration, the nanoprobes were extravasated through the compromised blood-brain barrier and then selectively phagocytosed by activated microglia, which subsequently migrated into the regions rich in dead neurons and neuronal debris. This microglia-mediated tropism decodes the signal origin of MRI enhanced by the nanometer-sized contrast agent, thereby transforming the MRI from an anatomical tool into a pathological reporter. A biocompatible Fe3O4 nanoparticle of similar size was also compared with the magnetic QD mentioned above for validating the translational merits of nanoparticles in MRI diagnosis of TBI.

title: A functional connectome identifies vulnerability to cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease progression.
abstract: Identifying the neurobiological basis of cognitive vulnerability is essential for preventing Alzheimer's disease (AD). We derived the Alzheimer's Resilience-Vulnerability Connectome (ARC) by contrasting SuperAgers (SA), an extreme phenotype of preserved late-life memory, with AD using resting-state fMRI. ARC distinguished SA from AD in a discovery cohort (N = 290; AUC = 0.85) and replicated independently (N = 143), involving prefrontal, temporal, and insular networks and associating with brain age. Applied to cognitively unimpaired adults (discovery: N = 818; replication: N = 497), ARC-based subtyping revealed SA-like and AD-like subgroups with comparable baseline cognition but divergent longitudinal trajectories. AD-like individuals exhibited faster cognitive decline, greater amyloid-β accumulation, and higher AD conversion risk. Exploratory GWAS nominated CLYBL and FRMD6 as candidate novel loci associated with the subtype difference. These findings suggest that ARC captures a continuous connectomic dimension of cognitive aging spanning SA, cognitively typical aging, and AD, highlighting the potential of functional connectomic variation for early risk stratification in AD.

title: METTL3-mediated m6A modification of DNMT1 enhances ovarian cancer progression.
abstract: High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC), the most lethal subtype of ovarian cancer, is often diagnosed at advanced stages and remains associated with poor clinical outcome. In this study, we identify a critical oncogenic role of the RNA methyltransferase METTL3 and the N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modification pathway in HGSOC. Suppression of METTL3, either genetically or pharmacologically, and depletion of its binding partner METTL14 impair ovarian cancer proliferation and tumor progression. Mechanistically, we show that METTL3-mediated m6A deposition enhances the translation of DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1), the primary maintenance DNA methyltransferase responsible for preserving genome-wide methylation patterns and silencing tumor suppressor genes. Pharmacological inhibition of DNMT1 induces widespread DNA hypomethylation and up-regulation of the tumor suppressors TNFAIP3 and FBXO32. Consistently, METTL3 suppression reduces DNMT1 abundance and derepresses TNFAIP3 and FBXO32 expression. Knockdown and rescue studies further reveal that DNMT1 primarily mediates METTL3-dependent regulation of cell migration, whereas the antiproliferative effects of METTL3 suppression are likely driven by additional downstream targets. Collectively, these findings identify the m6A-METTL3-DNMT1 axis as a mechanistic link between RNA and DNA methylation pathways and a potential therapeutic vulnerability in HGSOC.

title: Common transcriptional changes in the brain during hibernation and Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Hibernation demands rapid brain adaptations, involving cycles of reduced metabolic rate during torpor, followed by brief periods of arousal. Previous studies show hibernation induces a drastic increase in Tau hyperphosphorylation, but a mechanistic connection to disease remains unclear. Using single-nucleus RNA sequencing on hippocampi of golden hamsters, we unveil large transcriptional shifts across the hibernation cycle in all cell types, especially glia. Common transcriptional changes in mitochondrial and ribosomal genes are observed in all different cell types. In addition, hibernation triggers an inflammatory-like response in microglia that in part resembles cell states observed in Alzheimer's disease, but here in the absence of Aβ-accumulation and neurodegeneration. These findings reveal brain transformations that might help preserve vital functions under extreme conditions and they suggest that early cellular changes in AD may be a natural adaptive process.

title: N6-methyladenosine-dependent ARv7 translation couples lactate metabolism with enzalutamide resistance in prostate cancer.
abstract: Enzalutamide (Enz)-resistant prostate cancer (PCa) is a lethal disease that affects a broad population of elderly men. Experimental and clinical evidence has demonstrated that androgen receptor variant 7 (ARv7) plays a critical role in Enz-resistant (EnzR) PCa by functioning as a constitutively active transcription factor driving disease progression. However, the predictive value of the ARv7 transcript has not been fully recognized due to its low frequency in castration-resistant PCa. In this study, we identified ARv7 mRNA as an N6-methyladenosine (m6A)-modified transcript. Enz treatment increases METTL3-dependent m6A methylation of ARv7 mRNA at the A1177 site, which is subsequently recognized by the reader protein YTHDC2, leading to enhanced translation efficiency of ARv7. Furthermore, EnzR PCa exhibited elevated lactate metabolism, which regulated AR transcription through promoter-mediated epigenetic modifications at H3K9 and H3K14. Reactivated AR exhibited enhanced phase separation to transcriptionally up-regulate YTHDC2 expression. In vivo experiments demonstrated that targeting the METTL3-YTHDC2-ARv7 axis represents a promising therapeutic strategy to suppress EnzR PCa progression. Moreover, the METTL3 inhibitor STM2457 synergized with Enz to inhibit tumor growth without observable toxicity. Collectively, our findings suggest that the clinical utility of ARv7 may need to be reconsidered in light of its m6A-dependent translational regulation.

title: A disynaptic trigeminal circuit for the transformation and integration of oral chemesthesis in male mice.
abstract: Chemesthesis, encompassing oral sensations such as spiciness and coolness, is an important yet incompletely understood component of mammalian chemical sensing. Unlike taste or olfaction, these sensations are conveyed primarily through trigeminal pathways; however, how modality-specific peripheral signals are processed and transformed along central ascending pathways remains poorly understood. Herein, we delineate the structural and functional organization of an ascending trigeminal-brainstem-parabrachial circuit that mediates oral chemesthetic processing in male mice. Using viral tracing, in vivo calcium imaging, and chemogenetic and optogenetic manipulations, we identify a genetically defined disynaptic glutamatergic pathway (trigeminal ganglion → spinal trigeminal nucleus caudalis → lateral parabrachial nucleus) that is both necessary and sufficient for capsaicin- and menthol-evoked defensive behaviors. Although peripheral TRPV1+ and TRPM8+ neurons retain a degree of modality bias, we observe substantial convergence of spicy and cooling signals within the spinal trigeminal nucleus, followed by sustained and synchronized population activity in vglut2+ neurons of the external lateral parabrachial nucleus. This hierarchical transformation from peripheral segregation to central integration reveals the organizational principle by which distinct chemesthetic modalities are progressively integrated along a trigeminal-mediated ascending pathway, providing a circuit-level framework for understanding how chemical stimuli are processed and coordinated to drive defensive behaviors.

title: On-going retinal neuronal degeneration despite clinical stability in glaucoma.
abstract: Glaucoma, a leading cause of irreversible blindness, involves progressive retinal ganglion cell loss. Early detection of this neurodegeneration is critical, yet current clinical methods often identify disease only after substantial damage has occurred. This preliminary study used high-resolution adaptive optics-optical coherence tomography (AO-OCT) to track individual retinal ganglion cells in patients and healthy volunteers over 3 to 5 years. Results revealed higher neurodegeneration in glaucoma compared to normal aging. We observed 4.16 to 6.86% annual decrease in cell density in glaucoma, far exceeding the 0.27% cell loss rate observed in the healthy volunteer group. Critically, AO-OCT detected progression significantly earlier, identifying cell loss 0.74 years before conventional OCT and 1.49 years before visual field testing. These findings demonstrate AO-OCT as a more sensitive tool capable of monitoring glaucomatous damage with superior precision, potentially representing a major advancement over current clinical imaging.

title: A high robustness decoding technique for ultrasound modulated electroencephalogram.
abstract: Ultrasound-modulated electroencephalography (USMEEG) has become a vital tool in neuroscience because it integrates millimeter-level spatial resolution with millisecond-level temporal resolution. However, under extremely complex scenarios, excessively strong or weak acoustoelectric signal coupling leads to severe distortion in USMEEG decoded signals. To address this, we developed a highly robust decoding algorithm based on the ultrasound pulse repetition frequency and introduced the acoustoelectric modulation ratio (AMR) to quantify different modulation scenarios. Across numerical simulations, phantoms, and validation using human steady-state visual evoked potential signals with data-level acoustoelectric coupling across 10 volunteers, the focused ultrasound phased array achieved an encoding spatial resolution of 0.79 millimeters. The proposed algorithm significantly outperformed four traditional methods, exhibiting higher precision under weak modulation (0 1) conditions, with average decoding correlations reaching 0.84, 0.90, and 0.89. This highly robust technique expands USMEEG applications and provides a technical foundation for high-performance noninvasive brain-computer interfaces.

title: Shapley fields reveal mosaic chemotopic organization in the mouse Olfactory bulb across diverse chemical feature sets.
abstract: Neural representations in the olfactory bulb (OB) remain poorly understood compared to well-established coding principles in other sensory systems. This difficulty arises because a natural coordinate system for olfactory stimulus space has not yet been identified, complicating the characterization of neural receptive fields analogous to those in other sensory modalities. Moreover, the extent to which these tuning properties are spatially organized within the OB remains unclear. To advance our understanding of the olfactory coding, we introduce an interpretable method of Shapley fields, as an olfactory analog of retinotopic receptive fields. Shapley fields are spatial distributions of chemical feature importance for the tuning of OB glomeruli. We used this tool to investigate chemotopy in the OB with diverse sets of chemical features using widefield epifluorescence recordings of the mouse dorsal OB in response to stimuli across a wide range of the chemical space. We found that Shapley fields reveal a weak chemotopic organization of the chemical feature sensitivity of dorsal OB glomeruli. This organization was consistent across animals and mostly agreed across very different chemical feature sets: (i) the expert-curated PubChem database features and (ii) features derived from a Graph Neural Network trained on human olfactory perceptual tasks. This chemotopy involved at least three chemical feature dimensions, rather than one or two dominant properties. Moreover, we found that the principal components of the Shapley fields corresponded to single commonly accepted chemical classification groups. This implies that these chemical groups could have been identified purely from the mouse olfactory responses. Our findings suggest that Shapley fields may serve as a chemical feature-agnostic method for investigating olfactory perception.

title: Sibling Psychiatric Diagnoses and Risk of Postpartum Psychosis: A Nationwide Cohort Study.
abstract: Objective: To evaluate associations between sibling psychiatric diagnoses and risk of postpartum psychosis and to determine whether these associations vary by sibling sex and the woman's own psychiatric history. Methods: In this population-based cohort study using Swedish national registers, we identified 1,213,829 women with a full sibling who delivered their first live-born child between January 1980 and October 2017. The primary outcome was postpartum psychosis, defined as mania, psychosis, or psychotic depression within 90 days postpartum. Associations between sibling psychiatric diagnoses and postpartum psychosis were estimated using logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors, including stratification by the woman's own psychiatric history. Results: Overall, 1,831 women developed postpartum psychosis (1.5 per 1,000). The strongest associations were observed for sister's postpartum psychosis (OR=10.84; 95% CI, 5.76-20.40), cyclothymia (OR=8.29; 95% CI, 4.65-14.76), schizoaffective disorder (OR=7.90; 4.99-12.52), and bipolar disorder (OR=5.00; 95% CI, 4.23-5.90). Patterns were similar in brother and sister pairs. Sibling psychiatric history was most informative among women with no prior psychiatric diagnosis, where sibling schizoaffective disorder (OR=4.82; 95% CI, 2.99-7.74) and bipolar disorder (OR=3.07; 95% CI, 2.59-3.64) showed substantial risk increases. Among women with a history of mania or psychosis, sibling diagnoses contributed little additional predictive value. Conclusion: Postpartum psychosis shows strong familial aggregation across multiple sibling diagnoses, with a pattern supporting its conceptualization within the spectrum of severe mood disorders with psychotic features. Family psychiatric history may help identify at-risk women who lack established clinical predictors.

title: Ketamine/Esketamine in Clinical Practice: Areas of Consensus and Nonconsensus from an American Society of Clinical Psychopharmacology (ASCP) Delphi Panel Task Force.
abstract: Objective: Important aspects of ketamine/esketamine treatment for mood disorders in contemporary practice remain inadequately addressed by the current evidence base, necessitating expert guidance in areas where clinical decision needs and implementation have advanced more rapidly than available data. The American Society of Clinical Psychopharmacology convened an expert task force to address unresolved questions about the practical use of these agents in "real-world" settings and potential disparities with evidence-based literature. Participants: An international panel of 21 academic mood disorder psychopharmacologist-psychiatrists with expertise in ketamine/esketamine clinical care and research. Evidence: Consensus was reached on 35/105 items (33%), encompassing domains involving diagnostic conditions, contraindications, maximum dosing, racemic versus enantiomeric preparations, oral or intramuscular delivery formulations, laboratory/safety monitoring, access, and parameters for judging treatment outcome. Consensus Process: Two successive Delphi rounds were completed alongside multiple virtual, email, and in-person meetings. Consensus was defined a priori as ≥75% agreement/disagreement on 5-point Likert survey items. All authors contributed to the interpretation and drafting of recommendations. Conclusions: Consensus agreement appears elusive for many key decision points involving ketamine/esketamine treatment, reflecting substantial disparities between "real-world" clinical practice and the shortcomings of the clinical trials' evidence base. Uncertainties persist regarding the use of novel formulations (eg, oral or intramuscular), high-dose ketamine infusions, ketamine-assisted psychotherapy, and use in conditions other than major depression. These areas of expert consensus and dissent lay the groundwork for future studies urgently needed to bridge the gap between evidence-based findings and treatment implementation in routine clinical settings.

title: Establishing the Clinical Role of Digital Therapeutics in Major Depressive Disorder Treatment: A Consensus Panel Perspective.
abstract: Digital therapeutics for major depressive disorder (MDD) are evidence-based clinical interventions that can help address barriers in access to effective specialty/secondary care, patient preference for nonpharmacologic options, and continuity of care between visits. Despite growing evidence of efficacy, clinical adoption lags and current health care systems do not provide guidance for clinicians on their evaluation or implementation. In May 2026, a multidisciplinary expert consensus panel convened virtually to discuss the role of digital therapeutics in the management of MDD across primary care, specialty psychiatry, and community mental health practice in the United States and Europe. The panel developed four consensus statements regarding the evaluation, selection, and implementation of digital therapeutics for MDD. Digital therapeutics were identified as a distinct clinical category that should be evaluated using principles similar to other evidence-based MDD treatments, with efficacy as the primary selection criterion. Digital therapeutics may be incorporated across multiple stages of stepped-care management, including bridge-to-care and augmentation treatment. The panel identified clinician unfamiliarity, implementation challenges, and uncertainty regarding patient engagement as key adoption barriers. The consensus recommendations are intended to help clinicians select evidence-based digital therapeutics, position them appropriately within stepped-care management of MDD, and address the barriers preventing translation of current evidence into routine clinical practice.

title: Operationalizing independent oversight in large-scale public health cohorts: Monitoring protocol for the NIMHANS-NH-SKAN Stroke project.
abstract: onitoring the implementation of observational studies are rare, unlike experimental studies. This article aims to describe the development and implementation of a monitoring plan and framework for a large-scale cohort and quasi-experimental study: the NIMHANS-NH-SKAN Stroke project. The monitoring framework was developed through a systematic, stepwise process involving expert consultation workshops conducted by an Independent Monitoring Team in collaboration with the study team. A logical framework approach was used to identify key processes throughout the study implementation. These processes were then disaggregated into critical activities (sub-processes) to generate an initial list of monitoring items. These items were prioritized using the Vital-Essential-Desirable (VED) strategy through consensus building. The shortlisted items were further refined using SMART criteria (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound) to finalize checklist components. Key Performance Indicators were subsequently derived from the finalized checklist items. The framework emphasized usability, feasibility, and relevance to implementation, enabling systematic monitoring of critical study processes. A total of 89 activities were identified and consolidated into 10 checklists, from which 16 Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) were derived. The monitoring framework primarily emphasized indicator-based assessment of project outputs and outcomes while ensuring adherence to key processes and quality standards. KPIs were expressed as proportions to facilitate standardized performance assessment across sites and time periods. The checklists comprised a combination of in-person observations and record reviews. Monitoring findings were synthesized into periodic reports based on KPI proportions, enabling objective evaluation of implementation performance and identification of areas requiring corrective action. Timely and systematic monitoring is critical to ensure rigor in large-scale projects, and the approach described in this study provides a replicable framework for the development of robust monitoring systems in similar community-based large-scale observational studies in India and similar countries.

title: Computational modelling of acetylcholine deficiency-mediated dysfunction in the basal ganglia-thalamocortical network related to Parkinson's disease dementia.
abstract: Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) is a significant form of dementia. Its pathophysiology involves not only the dopaminergic system impairment but also the degeneration of cholinergic neurons in the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN), which is considered a potential contributor to the cognitive decline in PDD. Therefore, this study develops a computational model of the PPN-modulated basal ganglia-thalamic-cortical network to investigate how acetylcholine deficiency affects cortical oscillations. Based on anatomical evidence, acetylcholine deficiency is modeled by modulating synaptic connections from the PPN to the thalamus and basal ganglia output nuclei. Power spectrum analysis shows that acetylcholine deficiency, whether in the PPN-thalamic nucleus pathway or in the PPN-basal ganglia output nucleus pathway, leads to a decrease in cortical power ratio between the high-frequency band and low-frequency band. These results qualitatively reproduce the characteristics of electrophysiological measurements recorded in PDD. Further dynamical analysis suggests that this reduction may be associated with weakened oscillatory activity, reflected by a shift in neuronal firing patterns from limit cycle to point attractor. Moreover, simulations of combined acetylcholine and dopamine deficiencies reveal that both neurotransmitters can reduce the cortical power ratio, with a synergistic interaction rather than a simple additive effect. These findings provide a systems-level perspective on how ACh deficiency may contribute to cortical dysfunction in PDD and may offer a potential direction for future therapeutic research.

title: The effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition and influence of FTO genotype in exercise-trained men and women.
journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
abstract: High-protein diets have consistently been associated with favorable changes in body composition in both sedentary and exercise-trained populations. Despite abundant evidence supporting protein intakes above the recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for active individuals, the effects of deliberate protein overfeeding, particularly in those already consuming adequate protein, remain incompletely characterized. The primary purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition in exercise-trained men and women. The secondary purpose was to determine whether body composition adaptations differed by FTO rs9939609 genotype. Fifty-six exercise-trained men and women (age: 22.40 ± 5.78 years; body mass: 75.47 ± 14.98 kg; BMI: 24.52 ± 3.50 kg/m2; resistance training: 5.12 ± 3.35 h/week) were enrolled in a 4-week dietary intervention. Participants were instructed to increase their daily protein intake by approximately 20% above baseline while maintaining habitual training. Body composition was assessed pre- and post-intervention using a multi-frequency bioelectrical impedance device (InBody® 270). Dietary intake was self-monitored via MyFitnessPal®. Thirty-five participants completed both pre- and post-testing assessments and constituted the primary analysis. Linear regression models adjusted for baseline values indicated that FTO genotype was not a significant predictor of body composition changes (p > 0.05). Protein intake trended toward a significant increase over the 4-week period (pre: 146 ± 66 g/day vs. post: 164 ± 79 g/day; p = 0.053), representing an approximate 12% increase. Total energy intake, carbohydrate, and fat intake did not significantly change. Lean body mass increased significantly (pre: 59.95 ± 14.14 kg vs. post: 60.62 ± 14.42 kg; p = 0.005; Cohen's d = 0.31) and total body water increased significantly (pre: 43.85 ± 10.35 L vs. post: 44.34 ± 10.55 L; p = 0.005). Fat mass (p = 0.424), body fat percentage (p = 0.149), and total body mass (p = 0.09) did not significantly change. A 4-week modest protein overfeeding protocol in exercise-trained men and women was associated with a significant increase in lean body mass and total body water without concomitant increases in fat mass. These adaptations were not modified by FTO rs9939609 genotype. These findings support the contention that higher protein intakes do not promote fat accretion and may facilitate improvements in body composition in trained individuals.

title: Multiple hats, one truth: Lived experience as knowledge.
abstract: The global mental health field increasingly recognizes the importance of involving people with lived experience of mental ill-health in research, policy, services, and systems. However, recognition and representation have not consistently translated into meaningful authority. The current essay examines the conceptual and structural questions underlying this gap: what constitutes experiential knowledge; how lived experience is transformed into expertise; how experiential, clinical, academic, and policy knowledge interact; and how institutions can distinguish genuine co-production from symbolic participation or incognito tokenism. Drawing on participatory traditions within and beyond mental health and community-led practice, the essay argues that experiential knowledge is neither a substitute for professional expertise nor subordinate to it. Instead, these forms of knowledge should operate reciprocally, with epistemic authority shifting according to whose knowledge is most relevant to the question at hand. At the same time, the authors distinguish this fluid exchange of epistemic authority from the more entrenched institutional power governing resources, leadership, and decision-making. The essay examines how power, institutional readiness, context, crisis, and intersectional diversity shape whether participation becomes structural or merely symbolic. A case study from Nunavut, Canada, illustrates both the consequences of externally imposed systems and the possibilities created when Indigenous knowledge and authority determine terms of engagement. Practical recommendations for moving from consultation toward co-governance are put forward to support decision-makers within global mental health seeking to operationalize meaningful lived-experience engagement rather than simply endorse it.

title: The role of infant presence and other social correlates of fetal loss in wild mandrills.
abstract: The survival of offspring is an important determinant of fitness. A new study in PLOS Biology examines how early conceiving female mandrills (Mandrillus sphinx) with an infant have a higher probability of fetal loss, relative to other females.

title: Experiences of individually tailored physical exercise in COVID-19-induced postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome: A qualitative content analysis.
abstract: Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) is a phenotype of post-COVID-19 Condition (PCC), characterised by orthostatic intolerance and a range of debilitating symptoms. Exercise is a frequently implemented intervention in the treatment of POTS and PCC. However, patients' experiences with exercise as a therapeutic modality remain largely unexplored. This study aimed to explore the experiences of individuals diagnosed with PCC and POTS who underwent an individually tailored physical exercise intervention. A qualitative study design with an inductive approach was applied. Twenty-three participants who completed a feasibility study, involving semi-supervised tailored exercise, were recruited for individual interviews. Data were collected using a semi-structured interview guide and analysed through qualitative content analysis. Five main categories emerged, underscoring the importance of individualised design of exercise programs, flexible modalities, and continuous support from physiotherapists with expertise in PCC and POTS. Participants experienced improvements in physical, mental, and social functioning, although setbacks and symptom fluctuation were common. Strategies for energy management, alongside informal and formal support, were identified as facilitators and reduced barriers to exercise as a treatment. Psychological dimensions, including hope, motivation, goal setting, emotional adaptation, acceptance, and coping strategies, were central to participants' experiences. The combination of the intervention structure, therapeutic support, and effective strategies was perceived as contributing to the intervention's effectiveness, and many participants viewed exercise as a key pathway to recovery. This study highlights the need for a flexible and individualised rehabilitation approach in COVID-19-induced POTS. Moreover, exercise should be closely monitored by a physiotherapist with condition-specific expertise, who not only adapts the exercise to symptom fluctuations but also addresses diverse psychosocial needs and individual resources. The participants' experiences indicate that a holistic, multidisciplinary, and person-centred rehabilitation model may support recovery and contribute to improved long-term wellbeing in individuals with PCC and POTS.

title: Not all tRNAs are equal: how isodecoder diversity shapes cancer.
abstract: Several tRNAs that differ only in their body sequence decode the same codon, yet their levels and behavior vary across cell types and disease contexts. In a landmark 2014 study, a mutation in the arginine isodecoder Arg-TCT-4 was linked to neurodegeneration in mice. In 2021, increased expression of the Arg-TCT family, especially Arg-TCT-4, was unexpectedly linked to oncogenic transformation in multiple cancer models. A recent publication by Kim and colleagues reports that loss of a single tRNA isodecoder, Arg-TCT-1, drives lineage plasticity and resistance to androgen receptor pathway inhibitors in prostate cancer by reducing the translation of AGA-rich mRNAs. Together, these findings raise a broader question: what do differences in isodecoder sequence actually do? They may influence tRNA processing, charging, interactions with elongation factors and the ribosome, or the modifications tRNAs receive. This commentary places the new findings in the context of prior work and considers potential mechanisms behind the functional diversity of Arg-TCT isodecoders and their role in cancer.

title: Current Evidence Does Not Support Substantial DNA Cytosine Methylation in Myxosporean Genomes.
abstract: Some invertebrate lineages are known to have lost their ability to methylate DNA cytosines. These lineages have often lost the enzymes responsible for cytosine methylation (DNMT1 and 3), as well as other enzymes that interact with methylated cytosines. Previous studies showed that myxosporeans, a group of parasitic cnidarians, lack recognisable DNMTs and other canonical methylation enzymes, and observed a lack of cytosine methylation in two myxosporeans using whole genome bisulfite sequencing. Recently, a study of five myxosporean samples using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing reported high levels of methylation in two samples and low levels in the others and the presence of methylation-related genes in their assemblies. Here, we provide evidence that the two assemblies for which high levels of methylation were reported are heavily contaminated with fish-host sequences. In the other three samples, the lower apparent methylation signal resembles that observed in unmethylated negative controls and can be explained by ONT-background noise. Moreover, the CpG observed-to-expected ratios of the five assemblies differ from those of well-curated myxosporean assemblies. Additionally, the reported methylation profiles do not exhibit the typical distribution seen in invertebrates, possibly reflecting the presence of host contaminants. Finally, we found that most of the genes analysed are not canonical components of cytosine methylation pathways, and that the few candidate methylation-related genes reported in myxosporeans are more consistent with bacterial contamination than with genuine myxosporean genes. Together, these observations underscore important caveats in inferring the presence or absence of cytosine methylation in parasite genomes, particularly when using emerging technologies, and suggest that there is currently no robust evidence for substantial cytosine methylation in myxosporeans.

title: Protocol for generating nociceptor-enriched peripheral sensory neurons from human induced pluripotent stem cells.
abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) are a valuable system for studying human development, modeling disease-associated cellular phenotypes, and generating difficult-to-access cell types, such as sensory neurons (SNs). Here, we present a stepwise differentiation protocol for generating peripheral SNs from hiPSCs under defined culture conditions. We describe steps for expansion of hiPSCs, induction of neural crest cells (NCCs), dissociation and replating of NCCs, and maturation into SNs. This protocol yields nociceptor-enriched SN cultures.

title: Tau-driven hyperexcitability of locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons underlies sleep fragmentation and cognitive decline in mice.
abstract: Early sleep disruption is a hallmark of preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD), but its underlying mechanisms are unclear. The locus coeruleus (LC) dopamine-β-hydroxylase noradrenergic (LCDBH) neurons are vulnerable to early tau pathology in AD. Using P301S transgenic mice and cell-type-specific tau overexpression models, we show that pathological tau accumulation selectively increases the intrinsic excitability of LCDBH neurons. Tau-induced neuronal hyperactivity disrupts sleep homeostasis, reduces non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and slow-wave activity, increases sleep fragmentation and microarousals, and delays both anesthetic induction and sleep onset. Furthermore, tau overexpression in LCDBH neurons leads to significant recognition memory deficits. Notably, optogenetic suppression of LCDBH-tau neuronal activity reverses sleep disturbances and rescues cognitive dysfunction. Our findings demonstrate that tau-driven hyperexcitability of LCDBH neurons is a core driver of early sleep and cognitive impairments in AD, providing a mechanistic insight and potential target for preclinical AD treatment.

title: Plagl2 reprograms adult mouse retinal Müller glia for proliferation and injury-enhanced neurogenic competence.
abstract: Müller glia (MG) in the adult mammalian retina have long been recognized as a potential endogenous source for the regeneration of lost retinal neurons. However, existing MG reprogramming strategies yield an incomplete regenerative response by favoring either proliferation or neurogenic differentiation. Here, we show that the zinc-finger transcription factor gene Plagl2, previously shown to reactivate quiescent neural stem cells, is sufficient to reprogram adult mouse MG into a progenitor-like state with coupled proliferative and neurogenic competence. Using histology, time-lapse imaging, and single-cell transcriptomics, we find that Plagl2 drives regulated rounds of MG cell cycle re-entry, while N-methyl-D-aspartate-induced retinal injury further promotes the acquisition of neurogenic competence biased toward inner nuclear layer neuronal identities. These findings indicate that Plagl2 regulates mammalian MG reprogramming, and supports a broader approach to tissue regeneration through the adaptation of reprogramming modules across distinct cell types.

title: Cannabidiol and fronto-parietal EEG connectivity in autistic children.
abstract: Autistic children often show altered brain network connectivity, including circuitry implicated in social cognition. Cannabidiol (CBD) has emerged as a potential therapy for autism, but its neural mechanisms remain under-researched. Here, we analyze resting-state data collected as part of a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial, to explore whether 12 weeks of oral CBD oil could modulate functional connectivity in autistic children. Twenty-nine autistic children (5 to 12 years) completed two 12-week intervention periods (CBD and placebo, randomized) separated by an 8-week washout.
